courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: Instantaneous power in an AC circuit: p(t) = v(t)i(t) at every instant, so the DC relation P = VI survives only as an instantaneous statement and must be averaged over a whole cycle before it can be called the power

Decomposition of the instantaneous power: with v = V0 sin(wt) and i = I0 sin(wt - phi), p(t) = (V0*I0/2)[cos(phi) - cos(2wt - phi)], a constant term plus a ripple at twice the supply frequency whose average over a cycle is zero

The master formula P_av = (1/2)V0*I0*cos(phi) = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) = Irms^2 * R, so that only the resistance dissipates and a pure reactance consumes no average power however large its current and voltage

Real, reactive and apparent power distinguished: P = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) in watts, Q = Vrms*Irms*sin(phi) in volt-amperes reactive, S = Vrms*Irms in volt-amperes, forming a right-angled power triangle with S^2 = P^2 + Q^2 and tan(phi) = Q/P

Power factor PF = P/S = cos(phi) = R/Z, dimensionless and between 0 and 1, with the sign of phi carried separately as lagging (inductive, Q positive) or leading (capacitive, Q negative) since cos(phi) is an even function

The sign of the instantaneous power: p(t) oscillates about P with amplitude S, so its minimum S(cos(phi) - 1) is negative in any circuit with a net reactance and zero only when phi = 0; negative p means energy returning to the source, and for a pure L or C the positive and negative areas cancel exactly

Element by element: a resistor has p = P(1 - cos 2wt) swinging from 0 to 2P and never negative; an inductor has p = -Vrms*Irms*sin(2wt) with zero mean, storing up to (1/2)L*I0^2 in the magnetic field and returning it; a capacitor behaves identically with the electric field and the opposite sign of Q

Practical consequences: power-factor correction by a parallel capacitor with Q_C = P[tan(phi1) - tan(phi2)] and C = Q_C/(w*Vrms^2), which leaves P unchanged while cutting the line current and the I^2 R feeder loss; and series resonance at X_L = X_C, w0 = 1/sqrt(LC), where Z falls to R, PF = 1 and the real power Vrms^2/R is a maximum

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: The indefinite integral of f is the whole family of its antiderivatives: (integral of f(x) dx) = F(x) + C means F'(x) = f(x), and the arbitrary constant is there because any two functions with the same derivative differ by a constant

The power rule for integration, (integral of x^n dx) = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for every n except n = -1 - raise the power, then divide by the new power, after rewriting roots and reciprocals as powers - with the excluded case filled by (integral of dx/x) = ln|x| + C, whose modulus is needed because 1/x is defined for negative x while ln x is not

Integration is linear - it splits over sums and differences and lets constant multiples out - but there is no product, quotient or chain rule for integration, so products must be expanded, quotients divided out and composites substituted before anything can be integrated

Standard forms: sin x -> -cos x, cos x -> sin x, sec^2 x -> tan x, e^x -> e^x, e^(kx) -> e^(kx)/k, a^x -> a^x/ln a, and 1/(ax + b) -> (1/a) ln|ax + b|, where integration divides by the inner derivative exactly where differentiation multiplied by it, and only when that inner function is linear

Integration by substitution reverses the chain rule: setting u = g(x) with du = g'(x) dx turns the integral into one in u alone, which works only when the inner derivative is already present up to a constant multiple, and in a definite integral the limits must be converted to u-values or the answer converted back to x

The definite integral (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) is a number - the limit of the Riemann sums, sum of f(x_i*) times delta x - read either as the net signed area between the curve and the x-axis over [a, b] or as the total accumulated change of a quantity whose rate of change is f

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, d/dx of (integral from a to x of f(t) dt) = f(x) and (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) = F(b) - F(a) for any antiderivative F, together with the properties (zero width, reversal of limits, additivity over intervals, average value) and the split-at-the-roots method for total area as opposed to signed area

Applications: recovering a curve from its gradient function by fixing C from a given point, and recovering velocity and displacement from acceleration and velocity, where displacement is the integral of v and distance travelled needs the total-area treatment

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: A programme is a series of instructions that causes a computer or a microcontroller to perform a particular task; it also contains data and the memory addresses in which the instructions work, and is written in a programming language such as C, C++, Rust, Assembly, Java or Python

A data type is used for specifying the type of a variable; data types determine the type and size of the data associated with variables, and the three basic types in C are characters (char, 1 byte), integers (int, typically 4 bytes, exact within its range) and floating-point numbers (float 4 bytes, double 8 bytes, approximate to a fixed number of significant digits)

Variable definition always includes 'data type' followed by 'variable name'; a variable definition is also a declaration but not all declarations are definitions - a declaration gives the compiler a name and a type, a definition additionally reserves the storage, and 'extern int total;' declares without defining

The rules governing a variable name in C: letters, digits and the underscore only, never beginning with a digit, no spaces or other punctuation, never a keyword, and case-sensitive; and variable names are not stored inside the computer memory - the compiler replaces them with memory location addresses, so the name exists only at compile time

The six operator categories the course lists - arithmetic (+ - * / % ++ --), relational (== != > < >= <=), logical (&& || !), bitwise (& | ^ ~ << >>), assignment (= += -= etc) and misc (sizeof, address-of &, dereference *, ?: and the cast) - with relational and logical operators yielding the int 1 or 0 and assignment yielding the value it stored

Precedence and associativity: unary -> * / % -> + - -> << >> -> < <= > >= -> == != -> & -> ^ -> | -> && -> || -> ?: -> assignment -> comma, with the binary operators associating left to right and the unary operators, ?: and assignment associating right to left; short-circuit evaluation means && skips its right operand when the left is false and || skips it when the left is true

The operand types choose the operation, not the variable being assigned to: 7 / 2 is the int 3 because both operands are int and the fractional part is truncated towards zero, so a cast must be applied to an operand ((float) a / b) and never to the result ((float)(a / b)); and '5' is the char code 53, 5 is the int, and "5" is a two-character string

Programme objects: real-world objects have two main characteristics, state and behaviour, and in a programme the state of an object is stored in variables while the behaviour is described by methods; only the methods of a particular object have access to that object's variables, and different objects interact only through their own methods, which is information hiding and is controlled by the access specifiers public and private

Structures, unions and classes: a structure is a user-defined data type grouping items of possibly different types into a single type, defined with struct and accessed with the dot syntax, each member having its own storage; a union is defined the same way but all its members start at the same location in memory so it can represent the value of only one member at a time; a class is like a structure but also has methods or functions

Why use programme objects: objects are not dependent on each other so each can be independently created and maintained, an object can be used in various parts of the programme, a faulty object can be removed and replaced without disturbing the rest of the code (similar to how a car works), and because state is reachable only through methods we control how much we share with the outside world - giving modularity, code reusability and independence

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Aim of the experiment: study the discharge of a capacitor, determine the time constant tau, determine the experimental capacitance C, and calculate the percentage error for C

Theory of the capacitor: two conductors separated by a distance d with plate area A and a dielectric of permittivity epsilon, so C = epsilon*A/d; the stored charge is Q = CV; capacitors pass AC and block DC and are used as filters in DC supplies, energy-storage banks for pulsed lasers, timing control, backup power and voltage stabilisation

Discharge law: once the switch key is opened the capacitor voltage decays exponentially as V(t) = V0 * e^(-t/tau), the mirror of last week's charging law V(t) = V0 * (1 - e^(-t/tau)); at t = 0 the voltmeter reads maximum and the curve falls asymptotically to zero

Time constant: tau = RC in seconds with R in ohms and C in farads, and putting t = tau in the discharge equation gives V = V0 * e^(-1) = 0.3679*V0, so tau is the time for the voltage to fall to 36.8 percent of its maximum (against 63.2 percent gained when charging), with the capacitor effectively empty after about 5 tau

Apparatus and circuit: voltmeter, power supply, discharging circuit (capacitor, resistor, switch key), stopwatch and wires in the Praxilabs virtual RC Circuit Discharging laboratory, with the voltmeter connected in parallel across the capacitor

Procedure in order: connect the circuit, set the supply output voltage, close the switch key until the voltmeter reaches its maximum, then open the switch key and start the stopwatch at that instant, recording the voltmeter reading every 10 seconds for at least 7 (preferably 10) readings before ending the trial and downloading the data sheet

Data analysis and the two graphs: plot V on the y-axis against t on the x-axis and read tau where V = 0.3679*V0; then linearise as ln V(t) = ln V0 - t/tau and plot ln V against t to get a straight line of gradient -1/tau and intercept ln V0, the two values of tau having to agree

Calculations and errors: obtain C = tau/R and percentage error = (theoretical - experimental)/theoretical x 100, worked for the sample trial (V0 = 11 V, R = 15 kohm, nominal C = 2200 microfarads, theoretical tau = 33.0 s, graph tau about 32.9 s giving C about 2193 microfarads and 0.3 percent error), plus precautions and sources of error such as reaction time, voltmeter loading and dielectric leakage (both of which shorten the measured tau), lead resistance and component tolerance

courses.name: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
weekTopics: Human rights are rights inherent to all human beings regardless of race, sex, nationality, ethnicity, language, religion or any other status, and Article 1 of the UN Declaration of Human Rights holds that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, endowed with reason and conscience and bound to act towards one another in the spirit of brotherhood; they include the right to life and liberty, freedom from slavery and torture, freedom of opinion and expression, and the right to work and education

In Nigeria human rights are contained in Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution, Sections 33 to 46, and the African Charter on Human and People's Rights also guarantees that they are enforceable in Nigerian courts of law, the rights named for Nigeria being freedom of religion, freedom of speech, the right to education, freedom of movement and the right to life

A human rights abuse is anything that harms someone's human rights, including harm to people, communities and the environment; the 1979 Constitution introduced Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy alongside Fundamental Human Rights, shortcomings and inhibitions remain in the 2009 Rules, and the National Human Rights Commission received 1,701,519 cases of rights violations in 2021 against 1,287,280 complaints in 2020, the five common abuses named being extra-judicial killing, rape, restriction of freedom of expression, child marriage and domestic violence

Extra-judicial killing: the Nigerian security forces, particularly the police and military, have been implicated in extrajudicial killings, torture and excessive use of force, the #EndSARS protests of October 2020 brought international attention to police brutality, and the categories given are law enforcement officials, non-state actors, death sentences and deaths in custody due to the use of force or failure to protect the right to life

Rape is a serious human rights abuse in Nigeria, with about 367,000 women and gender-related issues recorded in 2021, obstructed by social stigma, underreporting of cases, inadequate legal frameworks, lack of access to justice and limited support services for survivors; and freedom of expression is restricted, with journalists threatened, intimidated, arrested and detained over political corruption and security, and much of the electronic media controlled through the National Broadcasting Commission's regulatory oversight of television and radio stations

Child marriage is prohibited under international law, and a State violates that law if it fails to establish a minimum age of marriage, enforce it, provide for and enforce the same minimum age for boys and girls, act with due diligence to prevent it, or if it involves public officials in it; 43% of girls in Nigeria are married before their 18th birthday and 16% before the age of 15 (Aliogo, 2023)

Domestic violence is addressed by the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act signed into law in 2015, which criminalises various forms of abuse and provides mechanisms for reporting, prosecution and support for survivors, though underreporting from social stigma, inadequate enforcement, limited awareness and inaccessible support services persist

The week's framing of democracy and the rule of law: democracy as government of the people, by the people and for the people, built on strong institutions rather than individuals or groups; the rule of law as governance by law rather than arbitrary decisions of officials, resting on supremacy of law, equality before the law and protection of individual rights through the courts; and Nigeria classified as a hybrid state on the Democracy Index, its democracy a work in progress, with the conclusion that human rights are not validated by the number of treaties a government has signed but by domestic enforcement, every agency being bound to enforce the norms of the Constitution and penalties being imposed regardless of socioeconomic class

courses.name: Communication in English II
weekTopics: Reading strategies defined as techniques and approaches used to enhance reading comprehension, retention and overall effectiveness with written text, helping the reader process information, extract meaning and gain deeper understanding, with SQ3R as one such strategy rather than the whole category
SQ3R read as S + Q + 3R and expanding to five stages in a fixed order: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review

Survey: quickly scanning the entire text before detailed reading, taking in headings, subheadings, images, captions and other structural features, to obtain a sense of the text's structure and main ideas

Question: generating your own questions from what the survey revealed rather than answering the questions supplied by the passage, so that the questions guide the reading and focus it on the most critical information
Read: the first full contact with the prose, with two stated goals - reading to answer the questions you generated, and reading to engage with the material for a fuller understanding

Recite: vocalising your thoughts by reciting or verbally explaining the key points, words and concepts in your own words, described in the summary slide as verbally or mentally summarising what you have learned to reinforce understanding

Review: creating summaries, outlines or notes and revisiting them and the text, the stage tied specifically to maintaining a deep understanding over time and being able to recall and apply it in exams or discussions

The supporting comprehension strategies from the week's summary sheet: context clues as in-text hints to the meaning of unfamiliar words, inference as a logical conclusion drawn from explicit details plus background knowledge, the fact/opinion distinction between the objective and verifiable and the subjective, and explicit meaning (directly stated, no inference) versus implicit meaning (suggested, requiring inference)

courses.name: Introduction to Web Technologies
weekTopics: The Document Object Model is a programming interface that represents an HTML, XHTML or XML document as a tree of objects, so scripts can read and change a page after it has loaded
DOM nodes come in three kinds that the exam distinguishes: element nodes (the tags such as div, button and a), attribute nodes (src, alt, id, class) and text nodes (the text inside an element)
The DOM tree is hierarchical: an element node has a parent node, child nodes and sibling nodes, and the text inside a paragraph is a text-node child of that paragraph rather than of its container
The document object is the entry point to the DOM and represents the whole page; document.title and every selection call start from it

Five selection methods and what each returns: getElementById -> one element or null, getElementsByClassName and getElementsByTagName -> a live HTMLCollection, querySelector -> the first CSS-selector match or null, querySelectorAll -> a static NodeList of all matches
Content modification with textContent (plain text, markup shown literally) versus innerHTML (parsed HTML), and the cross-site-scripting risk of assigning untrusted input through innerHTML

Attribute modification with getAttribute, setAttribute, removeAttribute and hasAttribute, plus custom data- attributes read through element.dataset, where data-user-id becomes dataset.userId and the value is always a string

Building and removing nodes with createElement (which produces a detached node), appendChild to attach it to the tree and parent.removeChild to take it out, and event handling with addEventListener("click", handler) where the handler is passed rather than called

questions.q: Find ∫x⁶ dx.
questions.concept: Power rule for integration
questions.why:
Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power: n = 6, so ∫x⁶ dx = x⁷/7 + c. Check: d/dx (x⁷/7) = 7x⁶/7 = x⁶.

7x⁷ multiplies by the new power instead of dividing; 6x⁵ differentiates instead of integrating; x⁵/5 lowers the power instead of raising it.

questions.q: Which of these functions has derivative 8x³?
questions.concept: Recognising an antiderivative by differentiating
questions.why:
Differentiate each candidate. d/dx (2x⁴ + 7) = 8x³ + 0 = 8x³, so 2x⁴ + 7 is an antiderivative of 8x³; the constant 7 disappears on differentiating, which is exactly why any constant may be added.

24x² is the derivative of 8x³, not a function whose derivative is 8x³; 8x⁴ differentiates to 32x³, the result of raising the power without dividing by 4; 4x⁴ differentiates to 16x³, the result of dividing 8 by 2 instead of by the new power 4.

questions.q: Find ∫5 dx.
questions.concept: Integrating a constant
questions.why:
Write 5 as 5x⁰ and use the power rule with n = 0: 5·x¹/1 + c = 5x + c. Check: d/dx (5x) = 5.

5 + c leaves the constant unchanged, which differentiates to 0, not 5; 0 is the derivative of a constant, not its integral; 5x²/2 treats the integrand as 5x instead of 5.

questions.q: Find ∫x⁻³ dx.
questions.concept: Power rule with a negative exponent
questions.why:
n = −3, so the new exponent is −3 + 1 = −2 and you divide by −2: x⁻²/(−2) + c = −1/(2x²) + c. The minus sign comes from dividing by the negative new power.

−3x⁻⁴ differentiates instead of integrating; 1/(2x²) forgets that dividing by −2 makes the answer negative; −1/(4x⁴) subtracts 1 from the exponent instead of adding it.

questions.q: F′(x) = 3x² and F(1) = 5. Find F(x).
questions.concept: Fixing the constant of integration from a given value
questions.why:
Integrate first: F(x) = ∫3x² dx = x³ + c. Then use the condition: F(1) = 1 + c = 5, so c = 4 and F(x) = x³ + 4. Check: F′(x) = 3x² and F(1) = 5.

x³ + 5 uses the given value 5 as c without evaluating x³ at x = 1; x³ drops the constant entirely, giving F(1) = 1; x³ − 4 has the sign of c wrong, from 1 + c = 5 solved as c = 1 − 5.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀² 3x² dx.
questions.concept: Definite integral by the Fundamental Theorem
questions.why:
An antiderivative of 3x² is F(x) = x³. By the Fundamental Theorem, ∫₀² 3x² dx = F(2) − F(0) = 8 − 0 = 8.

12 substitutes x = 2 into the integrand 3x² instead of into F; 24 uses 3x³ as the antiderivative, forgetting to divide by 3; 8 + c adds a constant to a definite integral, which is a number and carries no c.

questions.q: The graph of f(x) = 3 is a horizontal line at height 3. Evaluate ∫₁⁴ 3 dx, the area between the line and the x-axis from x = 1 to x = 4.
questions.concept: Definite integral as area under a horizontal line
questions.why:
F(x) = 3x, so ∫₁⁴ 3 dx = 3x|₁⁴ = 3(4) − 3(1) = 12 − 3 = 9. This is the rectangle of width 4 − 1 = 3 and height 3.

3 is the height of the line, not the area; 12 is F(4) alone, forgetting to subtract F(1); 15 adds F(1) instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: The power rule ∫xⁿ dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c is stated with the restriction n ≠ −1. What goes wrong at n = −1?
options: x⁻¹ is negative, so it cannot be integrated
x⁰ = 1, so the answer would be a constant
n + 1 = 0, so the formula divides by zero
questions.concept: Why the power rule excludes n = −1
questions.why:
At n = −1 the new exponent is n + 1 = 0 and the formula asks for x⁰/0. Division by zero is undefined, so the formula has nothing to say there; that is the only reason for the restriction.

x⁻¹ is not always negative and sign never blocks integration; x⁰ = 1 is true but the trouble is the denominator, not the numerator; 1/x does have an antiderivative, it is just not given by this formula.

questions.q: Find ∫√x dx by first writing √x as a power of x. State the value of n you use. Show your working.
questions.concept: Power rule with a fractional exponent
questions.why:
√x = x^(1/2), so n = 1/2. The new exponent is 1/2 + 1 = 3/2 and you divide by 3/2, which is the same as multiplying by 2/3: ∫x^(1/2) dx = x^(3/2)/(3/2) + c = (2/3)x^(3/2) + c. Check: d/dx (2/3)x^(3/2) = (2/3)(3/2)x^(1/2) = √x.

Final answer: (2/3)x^(3/2) + c. Also accepted: 2x^(3/2)/3 + c, (2/3)x√x + c, or 2√(x³)/3 + c. The working must show n = 1/2 and the division by 3/2. (3/2)x^(3/2) multiplies by the new power instead of dividing and is wrong; an answer without + c is incomplete.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₁² 2x dx twice: first using F(x) = x², then using F(x) = x² + 5. Show that both give the same number and say why. Show your working.
questions.concept: Constant of integration cancels in a definite integral
questions.why:
With F(x) = x²: F(2) − F(1) = 4 − 1 = 3. With F(x) = x² + 5: F(2) − F(1) = (4 + 5) − (1 + 5) = 9 − 6 = 3. The 5 is added at the upper limit and subtracted again at the lower limit, so it cancels: (F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c) = F(b) − F(a) for any c.

Final answer: 3 both times. A correct answer shows both evaluations reaching 3 and states that the added constant cancels in F(b) − F(a), which is why a definite integral never carries + c. Getting 8 for the second evaluation (adding 5 only once) is wrong.

questions.q: A student writes ∫x⁵ dx = 5x⁴ + c. Differentiate the student's answer to show it is wrong, name the mistake, and give the correct integral. Show your working.
questions.concept: Checking an antiderivative by differentiating
questions.why:
Differentiate the claimed answer: d/dx (5x⁴ + c) = 20x³, which is not x⁵, so the answer is wrong. The student differentiated instead of integrating (multiplied by the old power and lowered it). Integration goes the other way: raise the power to 6 and divide by 6.

Final answer: ∫x⁵ dx = x⁶/6 + c. Also accepted: (1/6)x⁶ + c. A correct answer shows the derivative 20x³ (or at least that it is not x⁵), says the student differentiated rather than integrated, and gives x⁶/6 + c. Check: d/dx (x⁶/6) = x⁵.

questions.q: Explain, using differentiation, why ∫2x dx = x² is an incomplete answer and ∫2x dx = x² + c is the full answer.
questions.concept: Why the constant of integration is required
questions.why:
The indefinite integral of 2x is every function whose derivative is 2x, not just one of them. Since the derivative of any constant is 0, [x² + c]′ = 2x + 0 = 2x for every real number c, so x² + 1, x² − 7 and x² + 100 are all antiderivatives of 2x. Writing x² alone names one member of the family and silently drops the rest; x² + c names them all.

A correct answer states that differentiating a constant gives 0, so x² + c has derivative 2x for every c, and concludes that the integral is the whole family x² + c, with c any real number.

questions.q: A 240 V rms supply drives 5.0 A rms through a load at power factor 0.80. Calculate the average (real) power consumed.
questions.concept: Real power from P = Vrms Irms cos φ
questions.why:
P = V_rms I_rms cos φ = (240)(5.0)(0.80) = 960 W.

1200 W is V I with the power factor left out, which is the apparent power S in VA, not watts; 720 W uses sin φ = 0.60 instead of cos φ and is the reactive power in var; 1500 W divides by the power factor instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A single-phase load is metered at 1.8 kW real power while drawing 2.4 kVA apparent power. Calculate its power factor.
questions.concept: Power factor as the ratio P/S
questions.why:
PF = P/S = 1.8/2.4 = 0.75. The power factor is the fraction of the volt-amperes drawn that does work, and it can never exceed 1.

1.33 is S/P, the ratio upside down, and is impossible because it is greater than 1; 0.66 is Q/S = sin φ, the reactive factor, with Q = √(2.4² − 1.8²) = 1.59 kvar; 0.88 is Q/P = tan φ.

questions.q: A motor draws an apparent power of 2500 VA and consumes 1500 W of real power. Calculate the reactive power.
questions.concept: Reactive power from the power triangle S² = P² + Q²
questions.why:
S² = P² + Q², so Q = √(S² − P²) = √(2500² − 1500²) = √(6 250 000 − 2 250 000) = √4 000 000 = 2000 var. It is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 500.

1000 var is S − P, subtracting the powers arithmetically, which the triangle forbids; 4000 var is S + P; 2915 var is √(S² + P²), adding inside the root instead of subtracting.

questions.q: A load draws an apparent power of 500 VA at a power factor of 0.60. The instantaneous power p(t) oscillates about its average value with amplitude S. Calculate the minimum value of p(t).
questions.concept: Minimum instantaneous power S(cos φ − 1)
questions.why:
p(t) = P − S cos(2ωt − φ) swings between P − S and P + S. The average is P = S cos φ = (500)(0.60) = 300 W, so the minimum is 300 − 500 = −200 W, that is, S(cos φ − 1). The negative part of the cycle is energy returning to the source.

−500 W is −S, forgetting that the swing is centred on P rather than on zero; +300 W is the average power, not the minimum; −400 W is minus the reactive power S sin φ, which is not a value p(t) takes on this basis.

questions.q: A supply voltage is v(t) = 170 sin(377t) V, with t in seconds. Calculate the frequency at which the instantaneous power delivered to a load pulsates.
questions.concept: Instantaneous power ripples at twice the supply frequency
questions.why:
ω = 377 rad/s, so the supply frequency is f = ω/2π = 377/6.283 = 60 Hz. The product v(t)i(t) contains cos(2ωt − φ), so the power completes two cycles for every one of the voltage: 2f = 120 Hz.

60 Hz is the supply frequency, forgetting the doubling; 377 Hz reads ω as if it were f, skipping the 2π; 754 Hz doubles ω but still never divides by 2π.

questions.q: An inductive load has a power factor of 0.50 lagging. Calculate the angle by which the current lags the supply voltage.
questions.concept: Phase angle from the power factor
questions.why:
PF = cos φ, so φ = cos⁻¹(0.50) = 60°. Lagging means the current reaches its peak 60° after the voltage does.

30° is sin⁻¹(0.50), using sin in place of cos; 26.6° is tan⁻¹(0.50); 28.6° reads 0.50 as an angle in radians and converts it to degrees.

questions.q: A 2.0 kW heater (PF = 1) and a 2.0 kW motor (PF = 0.50) each run from a 240 V rms supply. Calculate how much more rms current the motor draws than the heater.
questions.concept: Line current from real power and power factor
questions.why:
The cable carries S = P/PF, and I = S/V. Heater: I = 2000/240 = 8.33 A. Motor: S = 2000/0.50 = 4000 VA, so I = 4000/240 = 16.67 A. The difference is 16.67 − 8.33 = 8.3 A.

16.7 A is the motor's whole current, not the extra; 0 A assumes equal watts means equal amps, which holds only at equal power factor; 4.2 A multiplies by the power factor instead of dividing, so it makes the motor draw less than the heater.

questions.q: A load's power factor is quoted as simply 0.80, with no further information. Which one of the following can you NOT deduce from that number?
options: Whether the current leads or lags the voltage
The size of the phase angle between v and i
The fraction of the volt-amperes that does work
questions.concept: Power factor is even in φ: lagging versus leading
questions.why:
cos φ is an even function: cos(+36.9°) = cos(−36.9°) = 0.80. The number fixes P/S, the size of the angle (36.9°) and the fraction of S that is real power, but it cannot say whether φ is positive (inductive, current lags) or negative (capacitive, current leads). That is why a power factor is always written with the word lagging or leading attached.

The other three options are all exactly what PF = P/S = cos φ tells you directly.

questions.q: A supply v(t) = 100 sin ωt V drives a current i(t) = 4.0 sin(ωt − 60°) A through a load. Calculate the average power and the apparent power. Show your working.
questions.concept: Average power from peak values and phase angle
questions.why:
The amplitudes are peak values, so P = ½V₀I₀ cos φ = ½(100)(4.0)cos 60° = (200)(0.500) = 100 W. Equivalently V_rms = 70.7 V, I_rms = 2.83 A and P = (70.7)(2.83)(0.500) = 100 W. Apparent power S = ½V₀I₀ = V_rms I_rms = 200 VA.

Final answers: P = 100 W (accept 99 to 101 W) and S = 200 VA (accept 199 to 201 VA). Q = 173 var may be given as well but is not required. P = 400 W comes from using peak values without the ½ and dropping cos φ; P = 200 W drops cos φ only, which is S quoted as watts; both are wrong.

questions.q: A pure capacitor of reactance 25 Ω is connected across a 100 V rms supply. Calculate the rms current, the average power consumed and the reactive power. Show your working.
questions.concept: Average and reactive power of a pure reactance
questions.why:
I = V/X_C = 100/25 = 4.0 A. In a pure capacitor the current leads the voltage by 90°, so cos φ = cos 90° = 0 and the average power P = V I cos φ = 0 W: energy is stored in the electric field for a quarter cycle and returned in the next, and none is dissipated. The reactive power is Q = V I sin φ = (100)(4.0)(1) = 400 var, capacitive (leading), which may be written −400 var.

Final answers: I = 4.0 A, P = 0 W, Q = 400 var (accept 400 var capacitive, 400 var leading or −400 var). Also accepted: Q = I²X_C = (16)(25) = 400 var or V²/X_C = 400 var. Writing P = 400 W confuses reactive with real power and is wrong.

questions.q: With v = V₀ sin ωt and i = I₀ sin(ωt − φ), use the identity sin A sin B = ½[cos(A − B) − cos(A + B)] to write p(t) = vi as a constant plus one oscillating term. Hence show P = Vrms Irms cos φ. Show your working.
questions.concept: Deriving average power from the instantaneous power
questions.why:
p(t) = V₀I₀ sin ωt sin(ωt − φ). With A = ωt and B = ωt − φ, A − B = φ and A + B = 2ωt − φ, so p(t) = (V₀I₀/2)[cos φ − cos(2ωt − φ)]. The first term is a constant; the second is a sinusoid at 2ω whose average over any whole number of cycles is zero. So the average power is P = (V₀I₀/2) cos φ, and since V_rms = V₀/√2 and I_rms = I₀/√2, V_rms I_rms = V₀I₀/2, giving P = V_rms I_rms cos φ.

A correct answer must show the product form (V₀I₀/2)[cos φ − cos(2ωt − φ)], state that the cos(2ωt − φ) term averages to zero because it is a sinusoid over whole cycles, and convert V₀I₀/2 to V_rms I_rms. Writing the second term as cos(2ωt) without the φ, or claiming the ripple is at ω rather than 2ω, loses the derivation.

questions.q: The instantaneous power p(t) drawn by a load is measured and found to dip below zero for part of every cycle. Explain what a negative instantaneous power means physically, and whether this could happen for a purely resistive load.
questions.concept: Meaning of negative instantaneous power
questions.why:
p(t) = v(t)i(t) is the rate at which energy flows from the source into the load. A negative value means that, at that instant, energy is flowing back from the load to the source: the load's reactance (inductor or capacitor) is returning energy it stored earlier in its magnetic or electric field. It cannot happen for a pure resistor, because v and i are in phase there, so they are always both positive or both negative and their product is never negative. The minimum of p(t) is S(cos φ − 1), which is zero only when φ = 0.

A correct answer says negative p means energy returning to the source (not an error and not negative average power), attributes it to stored energy in a reactance, and states that a resistor's p(t) is never negative because v and i have the same sign at every instant.

checks.topic:
Data types, variables and programme objects, as concepts, exactly as the two decks give them.

What a programme contains besides its instructions. What a data type is, and the three basic types in C.

The deck's rule for a variable definition, and its sentence that a definition is also a declaration but not every declaration is a definition.

Why variable names are replaced by memory addresses. The six operator categories by name.

What a programme object is - state in variables, behaviour in methods, who may reach the state, and structure versus union versus class.

questions.q: Evaluate the C expression `30 - 8 / 4 * 2`, where every value is an int.
questions.concept: Operator precedence and associativity
questions.why:
`/` and `*` sit on the same level and associate left to right, and both outrank `-`: 8 / 4 = 2, then 2 * 2 = 4, then 30 − 4 = 26.

10 works strictly left to right, (30 − 8) / 4 * 2 with integer division; 29 does the multiplication first, 8 / (4 * 2) = 1; 56 does the subtraction first, (30 − 2) * 2.

questions.q: `int a = 17 / 5, b = 17 % 5;` What does `printf("%d %d", a, b);` print?
questions.concept: Integer division and remainder
questions.why:
Both operands are int, so `/` is integer division and the fractional part is thrown away: 17 / 5 = 3. `%` gives what is left over: 17 − 3 × 5 = 2. Output: 3 2.

3.4 2 performs real division although both operands are int; 4 2 rounds the quotient instead of truncating it; 2 3 swaps the quotient and the remainder.

questions.q: Which of these is a legal variable name in C?
questions.concept: Rules for a legal identifier
questions.why:
A name may use letters, digits and the underscore, must not begin with a digit, and must not be a keyword. `total_2` satisfies all three.

`2total` begins with a digit; `total-2` contains a hyphen, which C reads as the subtraction total − 2; `float` is a keyword and cannot be a name.

questions.q: `int a = 4, b = 7;` What is the value of `(a < b) + (a == b) + (b > 2)`?
questions.concept: Relational operators yield 1 or 0
questions.why:
Each comparison yields an int, 1 for true and 0 for false: a < b is 1, a == b is 0, b > 2 is 1, and 1 + 0 + 1 = 2.

3 counts a == b as true; 1 stops after the first comparison; 0 assumes a comparison has no numeric value and so cannot be added.

questions.q: What does `printf("%d %d", 1 && 2, 1 & 2);` print?
questions.concept: Logical versus bitwise operators
questions.why:
`&&` is logical: both operands are non-zero, so the result is 1. `&` is bitwise: 1 is 01 and 2 is 10, and no bit is set in both, so the result is 0. Output: 1 0.

1 1 treats `&` as if it were logical; 0 0 treats `&&` as if it were bitwise; 2 0 assumes `&&` returns one of its operands rather than 1.

questions.q: `int a = 5; int b = a++ + 2;` What are a and b after these two lines?
questions.concept: Post-increment yields the old value
questions.why:
`a++` yields the value a held before the increment, 5, and then makes a 6. So b = 5 + 2 = 7 and a = 6.

a = 6, b = 8 uses the value after the increment, which is what `++a` would do; a = 5, b = 7 forgets that `a++` changes a; a = 5, b = 8 makes both mistakes at once.

questions.q: `struct R { char name[16]; double value; };` and `union U { char name[16]; double value; };` With char 1 byte, double 8 bytes and no padding, what are `sizeof(struct R)` and `sizeof(union U)`?
questions.concept: Size of a structure versus a union
questions.why:
In a struct every member has its own storage, so the size is the sum: 16 + 8 = 24. In a union all members start at the same location, so the size is that of the largest member: the 16-byte array. Answer: 24 and 16.

24 and 24 gives the union separate storage for each member; 16 and 16 drops the double from the struct; 24 and 8 takes the double as the union's largest member, but the 16-byte array is bigger.

questions.q: A BankAccount object has `owner`, `balance`, `deposit()` and `withdraw()`. Which two make up its state?
questions.concept: State versus behaviour of an object
questions.why:
The state of an object is what it holds, stored in variables; its behaviour is what it does, described by methods. `owner` and `balance` are values the account holds, so they are its state. `deposit()` and `withdraw()` are actions, so they are behaviour.

The other pairings mix a variable with a method or list only methods.

questions.concept: Tracing a sequence of assignments
questions.why:
Line 2: c = 3 × 10 + 2 = 32 (a = 3, b = 10, c = 32). Line 3: b = 10 − 3 = 7 (a = 3, b = 7, c = 32). Line 4: a = 32 / 7, integer division, so 4 (a = 4, b = 7, c = 32). Line 5: c = 32 − 4 × 7 = 32 − 28 = 4 (a = 4, b = 7, c = 4).

Final answer: a = 4, b = 7, c = 4. A correct answer shows the value after every line, treats `b -= a` as b = b − a, and truncates 32 / 7 to 4 rather than 4.57. a = 4.57 or c = 0 (from 32 − 4.57 × 7) is wrong.

questions.q: a = 25 and b = 14. Write both as 8-bit binary and compute `a & b`, `a | b` and `a ^ b`, giving each result in decimal. Show your working.
questions.concept: Bitwise AND, OR and XOR
questions.why:
25 = 0001 1001 and 14 = 0000 1110. AND keeps a bit only where both are 1: 0000 1000 = 8. OR keeps a bit where either is 1: 0001 1111 = 31. XOR keeps a bit where exactly one is 1: 0001 0111 = 23.

Final answer: a & b = 8, a | b = 31, a ^ b = 23. A correct answer shows both binary strings and the bit-by-bit result for each operator. Treating `&` and `|` as logical (giving 1 and 1) is wrong.

questions.q: Classify each of these operators into one of the six categories (arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, assignment, misc): `%`, `>=`, `&&`, `<<`, `+=`, `sizeof`. Then state the value of `9 % 4 >= 1`.
questions.concept: Operator categories
questions.why:
`%` is arithmetic (remainder); `>=` is relational; `&&` is logical; `<<` is bitwise (left shift); `+=` is assignment; `sizeof` is misc. For the expression, `%` outranks `>=`: 9 % 4 = 1, and 1 >= 1 is true, so the value is 1.

A correct answer names all six categories correctly and gives 1 (also accepted: true). Calling `<<` arithmetic or `sizeof` a function is wrong; the value 0 comes from grouping as 9 % (4 >= 1) = 9 % 1 = 0, which ignores precedence.

questions.q: `int total;` and `extern int total;` both name the same variable and the same type. Explain why the first is a definition and the second is only a declaration, and say what a definition does that a declaration does not.
questions.concept: Declaration versus definition
questions.why:
A declaration tells the compiler a name and its type. A definition does that and also reserves the storage: bytes are set aside for the variable. `int total;` sets aside an int's worth of memory, so it defines and, in doing so, also declares. `extern int total;` says the variable exists and is an int but that its storage is reserved elsewhere, so it declares without defining.

A correct answer says every definition is also a declaration, that the difference is reserving storage (memory), and that `extern` marks a declaration that does not reserve any. Saying the difference is initialisation is wrong: `int total;` defines without initialising.

checks.topic:
Problems-only session on Week 7 integration.

Apply ∫xⁿdx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c to polynomials, negative powers, and fractions rewritten as powers.

Then evaluate definite integrals by the Fundamental Theorem, F(x)|ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a).

Includes both tasks the lecturer set — ∫(2x² − 6x − 3)dx and ∫₋₁²(7x − 5)dx.

Plus limits that are negative, antiderivatives that carry a minus sign, and one worked solution to diagnose.

questions.q: Find ∫(2x + 1)² dx.
questions.concept: Expanding before integrating
questions.why:
Expand first: (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1. Then integrate term by term: 4x³/3 + 4x²/2 + x + c = (4/3)x³ + 2x² + x + c. (The form (2x + 1)³/6 + c is the same family, since it expands to (4/3)x³ + 2x² + x + 1/6.)

(2x + 1)³/3 applies the power rule to 2x + 1 as if it were x and ignores the factor 2 inside; 4x³ + 4x² + x raises each power but never divides; (4/3)x³ + 4x² + x divides the first term but forgets to divide 4x by 2.

questions.q: Find ∫(x² + 1/x²) dx.
questions.concept: Integrating positive and negative powers together
questions.why:
Write 1/x² as x⁻². Then ∫x² dx = x³/3 and ∫x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/(−1) = −1/x, so the integral is x³/3 − 1/x + c. Check: d/dx (x³/3 − 1/x) = x² + 1/x².

x³/3 + 1/x loses the minus sign that comes from dividing by −1; 2x − 2/x³ differentiates instead of integrating; x³/3 − 1/(3x³) subtracts 1 from the exponent of x⁻² instead of adding it.

questions.q: Find ∫(6/x⁴) dx.
questions.concept: Rewriting a fraction as a negative power
questions.why:
Rewrite 6/x⁴ as 6x⁻⁴, so n = −4. The new exponent is −3 and you divide by −3: 6·x⁻³/(−3) + c = −2x⁻³ + c = −2/x³ + c. Check: d/dx (−2x⁻³) = 6x⁻⁴.

2/x³ loses the minus sign from dividing by −3; −6/(5x⁵) lowers the exponent to −5 instead of raising it to −3; −24/x⁵ differentiates 6x⁻⁴ instead of integrating it.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₋₁³ (2x − 4) dx.
questions.concept: Definite integral with a negative lower limit
questions.why:
F(x) = x² − 4x. F(3) = 9 − 12 = −3. F(−1) = (−1)² − 4(−1) = 1 + 4 = 5. So the integral is F(3) − F(−1) = −3 − 5 = −8. A negative answer is legitimate: 2x − 4 is below the axis for most of [−1, 3].

0 comes from writing −4(−1) as −4, giving F(−1) = −3; 8 subtracts in the wrong order, F(−1) − F(3); −3 is F(3) alone, forgetting the lower limit.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₁³ (2/x²) dx.
questions.concept: Definite integral of a negative power
questions.why:
Rewrite 2/x² as 2x⁻², so F(x) = 2x⁻¹/(−1) = −2/x. Then (−2/x)|₁³ = −2/3 − (−2) = −2/3 + 2 = 4/3. Factoring the minus out: −2(1/3 − 1) = −2(−2/3) = 4/3.

−4/3 uses +2/x as the antiderivative, losing the sign from dividing by −1; −8/3 adds F(1) instead of subtracting it, −2/3 + (−2); −16/9 substitutes into the integrand 2/x² instead of into F.

questions.q: Find the number b > 0 for which ∫₀ᵇ 2x dx = 25.
questions.concept: Solving for an unknown limit of integration
questions.why:
F(x) = x², so ∫₀ᵇ 2x dx = b² − 0 = b². Set b² = 25, and since b > 0, b = 5. Check: ∫₀⁵ 2x dx = 25 − 0 = 25.

25/2 solves 2b = 25, substituting the limit into the integrand 2x instead of into F; 5/√2 uses 2x² as the antiderivative, solving 2b² = 25; 25 forgets to take the square root of b² = 25.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₁⁴ (1/√x) dx.
questions.concept: Definite integral with a root in the denominator
questions.why:
Rewrite 1/√x as x^(−1/2). The new exponent is 1/2 and you divide by 1/2, which doubles: F(x) = 2x^(1/2) = 2√x. Then 2√x|₁⁴ = 2(2) − 2(1) = 4 − 2 = 2.

1/2 multiplies by the new exponent 1/2 instead of dividing, using F = (1/2)√x; 4 is F(4) alone, forgetting the lower limit; 1 uses F = √x, forgetting to divide by 1/2.

questions.q: Which of these rewritings of an integral is NOT justified by splitting and constant multiples?
questions.concept: What linearity of the integral licenses
questions.why:
Splitting licenses sums, differences and constant multiples only. The integral of a product is not the product of the integrals: ∫x³·x dx = ∫x⁴ dx = x⁵/5 + c, while (x⁴/4)(x²/2) = x⁶/8, which is not even the right power of x.

The sum, the difference and the constant multiple rewritings are all valid, because integration is linear.

questions.q: Find ∫(2x² + 3x − 4) dx and check your answer by differentiating. Show your working.
questions.concept: Integrating a polynomial term by term
questions.why:
Split the integral and apply the power rule to each term: ∫2x² dx = 2x³/3, ∫3x dx = 3x²/2, ∫4 dx = 4x. So ∫(2x² + 3x − 4) dx = (2/3)x³ + (3/2)x² − 4x + c. Check: d/dx [(2/3)x³ + (3/2)x² − 4x] = 2x² + 3x − 4.

Final answer: (2/3)x³ + (3/2)x² − 4x + c. Also accepted: 2x³/3 + 3x²/2 − 4x + c. The working must show each term divided by its new power and the differentiation check. 2x³ + 3x² − 4x + c (no division) and (2/3)x³ + (3/2)x² − 4 + c (constant not integrated to 4x) are wrong; an answer without + c is incomplete.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₋₂¹ (3x² − 2) dx. Show the substitution at x = −2 term by term. Show your working.
questions.concept: Definite integral with a cubed negative limit
questions.why:
F(x) = x³ − 2x. At x = 1: 1 − 2 = −1. At x = −2: (−2)³ − 2(−2) = −8 + 4 = −4. So ∫₋₂¹ (3x² − 2) dx = F(1) − F(−2) = −1 − (−4) = −1 + 4 = 3.

Final answer: 3. A correct answer states F(x) = x³ − 2x, shows (−2)³ = −8 and −2(−2) = +4 at the lower limit, and subtracts F(−2) = −4 to get 3. Taking (−2)³ as +8 gives F(−2) = 12 and the wrong answer −13; writing −2(−2) = −4 gives F(−2) = −12 and the wrong answer 11.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₁² (x² − 1)/x² dx by first dividing each term of the numerator by x². Show your working.
questions.concept: Dividing before integrating a definite integral
questions.why:
Divide: (x² − 1)/x² = x²/x² − 1/x² = 1 − x⁻². Integrate: F(x) = x − x⁻¹/(−1) = x + 1/x. Evaluate: F(2) = 2 + 1/2 = 5/2, F(1) = 1 + 1 = 2, so the integral is 5/2 − 2 = 1/2.

Final answer: 1/2 (also accepted: 0.5). The working must show the rewrite to 1 − x⁻², the antiderivative x + 1/x with the plus sign (from dividing x⁻² by −1 and then subtracting), and F(2) − F(1). Using x − 1/x as F gives 3/2 − 0 = 3/2 and is wrong; integrating numerator and denominator separately is not a valid method.

questions.q: A student evaluates ∫₀³ 6x dx as 6x|₀³ = 18 − 0 = 18. Explain what the student substituted the limits into, why that is wrong, and give the correct value.
questions.concept: Substituting limits into the antiderivative, not the integrand
questions.why:
The Fundamental Theorem says ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is an antiderivative of f. The student substituted the limits into f(x) = 6x itself; the limits must go into F(x) = 3x². Correctly: 3x²|₀³ = 3(9) − 3(0) = 27.

A correct answer says the limits were put into the integrand instead of the antiderivative, states F(x) = 3x² (from integrating 6x), and gives 27. Also accepted: 3(3² − 0²) = 27. An answer that only says the arithmetic is wrong, without naming F, is incomplete.

checks.topic:
Numerical work on power in an A.C. circuit.

Substituting into X_L = 2*pi*f*L and X_C = 1/(2*pi*f*C), then computing Z, I and cos(phi).

Then P = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) = Irms^2 R with Q and S, checking by S^2 = P^2 + Q^2.

Then power-factor correction, resonance and instantaneous-power calculations.

questions.q: A 15 Ω resistor is in series with a 159 μF capacitor across a 150 V rms, 50 Hz supply. Calculate the rms current.
questions.concept: Current in a series RC circuit via X_C = 1/(2πfC)
questions.why:
X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 159 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/0.0500 = 20.0 Ω. Z = √(R² + X_C²) = √(15² + 20²) = √625 = 25 Ω. I = V/Z = 150/25 = 6.0 A.

10 A is 150/15, ignoring the capacitor; 7.5 A is 150/20, ignoring the resistor; 4.3 A is 150/(15 + 20), adding R and X arithmetically instead of in quadrature.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 8.0 Ω, X_L = 22 Ω and X_C = 16 Ω. Calculate its impedance.
questions.concept: Impedance of a series RLC circuit with reactances subtracting
questions.why:
The two reactances are 180° apart, so they subtract: X = X_L − X_C = 22 − 16 = 6.0 Ω. Then Z = √(R² + X²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10 Ω.

39 Ω adds the reactances before squaring, √(8² + 38²); 46 Ω adds all three arithmetically; 14 Ω adds R and the net X arithmetically instead of in quadrature.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 9.0 Ω, X_L = 4.0 Ω and X_C = 16 Ω. Calculate its power factor and state whether the current leads or lags.
questions.concept: Power factor cos φ = R/Z with leading or lagging
questions.why:
X = X_L − X_C = 4.0 − 16 = −12 Ω. The net reactance is capacitive, so the current leads. Z = √(9² + 12²) = √225 = 15 Ω and PF = R/Z = 9/15 = 0.60 leading.

0.60 lagging has the right number but ignores the sign of X: with X_C larger than X_L the circuit is capacitive, not inductive; 0.80 is X/Z = 12/15, the reactive factor sin φ; 1.67 is Z/R, upside down, and no power factor can exceed 1.

questions.q: A series circuit carries 3.0 A rms through X_L = 30 Ω and X_C = 10 Ω. Calculate the net reactive power.
questions.concept: Net reactive power Q = I²(X_L − X_C)
questions.why:
The inductor absorbs I²X_L = (9)(30) = 270 var while the capacitor supplies I²X_C = (9)(10) = 90 var, and the two swap energy with each other, so they subtract: Q = I²(X_L − X_C) = 9 × 20 = 180 var, inductive.

360 var adds the two reactive powers instead of subtracting; 270 var is the inductor's share alone, forgetting the capacitor; 60 var is I × X without squaring the current.

questions.q: A 12 Ω resistor is in series with a reactance of 16 Ω across a 100 V rms supply. Calculate the real power dissipated.
questions.concept: Real power P = I²R in a series circuit
questions.why:
Z = √(12² + 16²) = 20 Ω, I = 100/20 = 5.0 A, and only the resistance dissipates: P = I²R = (25)(12) = 300 W. Check: V_R = IR = 60 V and V_R²/R = 3600/12 = 300 W.

833 W is V²/R with the full supply voltage, but only 60 V of the 100 V sits across R; 500 W is V I = S, the apparent power, with the power factor 0.60 forgotten; 400 W is I²X = 25 × 16, the reactive power in var.

questions.q: R = 20 Ω, L = 0.10 H and C = 40 μF are in series across a 120 V rms supply whose frequency is set to the resonant frequency. Calculate the rms current.
questions.concept: Current at series resonance, Z = R
questions.why:
ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(0.10 × 40 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/√(4 × 10⁻⁶) = 500 rad/s, at which X_L = ω₀L = 50 Ω and X_C = 1/(ω₀C) = 50 Ω. They cancel, Z = R = 20 Ω, and I = 120/20 = 6.0 A, the maximum this circuit can draw.

1.2 A adds the two reactances instead of cancelling them, giving Z = √(20² + 100²) = 102 Ω; 2.4 A is 120/X_L, using one reactance as the impedance; 0 A confuses the cancelling of X_L and X_C with the circuit being open.

questions.q: A 10 Ω resistor is connected across v(t) = 50 sin(100πt) V, with t in seconds. Calculate the instantaneous power at t = 1.0 ms.
questions.concept: Instantaneous power at a given time
questions.why:
At t = 1.0 × 10⁻³ s the phase is ωt = 100π × 0.001 = 0.1π rad = 18°, so v = 50 sin 18° = 50 × 0.309 = 15.45 V. Then p = v²/R = 15.45²/10 = 23.9 W ≈ 24 W (equivalently i = v/R = 1.545 A and p = vi).

125 W is the average power V₀²/2R, not the value at this instant; 226 W uses cos in place of sin (v = 47.6 V); 7.5 × 10⁻³ W comes from a calculator left in degree mode, evaluating sin(0.314°) instead of sin(0.314 rad).

questions.q: A series RLC circuit is driven at a frequency below its resonant frequency. Compared with resonance, what are its power factor and the phase of its current?
questions.concept: Power factor and phase of a series RLC circuit off resonance
questions.why:
Below resonance ω is small, so X_L = ωL is small and X_C = 1/ωC is large: the net reactance is capacitive, Z exceeds R, PF = R/Z drops below 1, and the current leads the voltage.

Lagging would need X_L greater than X_C, which happens above resonance; PF = 1 with the current in phase is the resonance condition itself; a power factor greater than 1 is impossible because R can never exceed Z.

questions.q: A coil of resistance 24 Ω and inductance 57.3 mH is connected across a 120 V rms, 50 Hz supply. Calculate X_L, Z, the rms current, the power factor, and P, Q and S, then check that S² = P² + Q². Show your working.
questions.concept: Complete power set for a series RL circuit with cross-check
questions.why:
X_L = 2πfL = 2π(50)(0.0573) = 18.0 Ω. Z = √(24² + 18²) = √900 = 30.0 Ω. I = V/Z = 120/30 = 4.00 A. PF = cos φ = R/Z = 24/30 = 0.800 lagging (φ = 36.9°, inductive, so the current lags). P = V I cos φ = (120)(4.00)(0.800) = 384 W, and by the second route I²R = (16)(24) = 384 W. Q = V I sin φ = (120)(4.00)(0.600) = 288 var inductive, and I²X_L = (16)(18) = 288 var. S = V I = 480 VA. Check: 384² + 288² = 147 456 + 82 944 = 230 400 = 480².

Final answers: X_L = 18.0 Ω, Z = 30.0 Ω, I = 4.00 A, PF = 0.80 lagging, P = 384 W, Q = 288 var, S = 480 VA (accept each within 1%). V²/R = 600 W is not the real power, because only V_R = IR = 96 V sits across the resistance; a student who writes 600 W has used the wrong voltage.

questions.q: A workshop draws 6.0 kW from a 240 V rms, 50 Hz supply at a power factor of 0.75 lagging. Calculate the apparent power, the line current and the reactive power. Then calculate the parallel capacitance that raises the power factor to unity, and the new line current. Show your working.
questions.concept: Power factor correction with a parallel capacitor
questions.why:
S = P/PF = 6000/0.75 = 8000 VA, and I = S/V = 8000/240 = 33.3 A. Q = √(S² − P²) = √(8000² − 6000²) = √(28 × 10⁶) = 5292 var lagging (equivalently S sin φ with sin φ = 0.661). For unity power factor the capacitor must supply all of it: Q_C = 5292 var, so C = Q_C/(ωV²) = 5292/[(314.2)(240²)] = 5292/(1.81 × 10⁷) = 2.92 × 10⁻⁴ F = 292 μF. The real power is unchanged, so the new line current is I = P/V = 6000/240 = 25.0 A.

Final answers: S = 8.0 kVA, I = 33.3 A, Q = 5.29 kvar (accept 5.25 to 5.35), C = 292 μF (accept 285 to 300 μF), new I = 25.0 A. A correct answer must show that P stays at 6.0 kW while the current falls from 33.3 A to 25.0 A. Using f = 50 instead of ω = 314 in C = Q/(ωV²) gives 1840 μF and is wrong.

questions.q: R = 25 Ω, L = 0.50 H and C = 8.0 μF are in series across a 100 V rms, 50 Hz supply. Calculate X_L, X_C, Z, the rms current, the power factor and the real power. State whether the current leads or lags and whether 50 Hz is above or below resonance. Show your working.
questions.concept: Series RLC power off resonance
questions.why:
X_L = 2πfL = (314.2)(0.50) = 157 Ω. X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/[(314.2)(8.0 × 10⁻⁶)] = 398 Ω. Net X = 157 − 398 = −241 Ω (capacitive), so Z = √(25² + 241²) = √(625 + 57 990) = 242 Ω. I = 100/242 = 0.413 A. PF = R/Z = 25/242 = 0.103 leading. P = I²R = (0.413)²(25) = 4.27 W. Since X_C exceeds X_L the current leads and 50 Hz is below the resonant frequency (f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 79.6 Hz).

Final answers: X_L = 157 Ω, X_C = 398 Ω, Z = 242 Ω, I = 0.41 A (accept 0.40 to 0.42), PF = 0.10 leading, P = 4.3 W (accept 4.1 to 4.4 W), current leading, below resonance. Adding the reactances to get X = 555 Ω, or using V²/R = 400 W for the power, is wrong; 400 W is what the circuit would consume only at resonance.

questions.q: For a series RL circuit on a 200 V rms supply, one student calculates the real power as V²/R using 200 V, and another as I²R. Explain why the two answers differ, which one is correct, and what voltage would make the V²/R form correct.
questions.concept: Why P = I²R is safe and V²/R with the supply voltage is not
questions.why:
P = V²/R assumes that the whole voltage V sits across the resistance. In a series RL circuit the supply voltage is shared between R and X_L in quadrature, so the resistor only has V_R = IR across it, which is less than 200 V. Using 200 V in V²/R therefore overestimates the power by the factor (Z/R)². P = I²R is always correct because the same current flows through every series element and only the resistance dissipates energy.

A correct answer says the supply voltage is not the voltage across R, that I²R is right, and that V²/R would be right only with V_R = IR (the resistor's own drop, or the supply voltage in a purely resistive circuit or at resonance). Saying that both formulas are always equivalent because they are in DC is wrong.

checks.topic:
Applied work on this week's material.

Writing a definition in the deck's required order, and reaching a member with the dot syntax.

Reading struct, union and class code from the week's summary sheet, and deciding what a union can hold at one time.

Separating an object's state from its behaviour on a new example.

Then data encapsulation with public and private, and representing a problem as data.

questions.concept: Casting before integer division
questions.why:
The operand types decide the division. Casting `sum` to float before the `/` makes it real division: 90.0 / 4 = 22.5.

`(float)(sum / count)` divides in int first, giving 22, and only then converts; `sum / count * 1.0` also divides in int before the 1.0 arrives, 22 * 1.0 = 22.0; changing the variable to double changes where the result is stored, not how it is computed.

questions.q: `struct Point { int x; int y; };` and `struct Point p;` have been written. Which line sets the x member of p to 4?
questions.concept: Accessing a member with the dot syntax
questions.why:
A member is reached by writing the variable, a dot, then the member name: `p.x = 4;`.

`x.p` puts the member before the variable; `Point.x` names the type rather than a variable, and no storage belongs to a type; `p(x)` is a function call, not member access.

questions.concept: A union holds one member at a time
questions.why:
All members of a union start at the same memory location. Writing 5 into b overwrites the bytes that held a, and since both are int, reading a now gives 5 too. Output: 5 5.

3 5 treats the union as a struct with separate storage; 3 3 has the overwrite going the wrong way, as if the first write won; 8 8 adds the two writes together.

questions.q: `int x = 7; x += 5; x *= 3; x %= 7;` What is x afterwards?
questions.concept: Compound assignment operators
questions.why:
`a op= b` means a = a op b, applied in order: x = 7 + 5 = 12; x = 12 × 3 = 36; x = 36 % 7 = 1.

36 stops before the `%=`; 7 reads `x %= 7` backwards as 7 % 36; 5 applies the `*= 3` before the `+= 5`, giving (21 + 5) % 7.

questions.concept: Copying a structure variable
questions.why:
`struct P b = a;` copies every member into b's own storage, so a and b are two separate objects. Changing b.x to 9 leaves a.x at 1. Output: 1 9.

9 9 assumes a and b share one location, which is what a union would do; 1 1 forgets that the assignment to b.x happened; 9 1 puts the change on the wrong variable.

questions.q: `char c = '7';` What does `printf("%d %d", c, c - '0');` print?
questions.concept: Character codes versus digit values
questions.why:
A char holds a character as a small integer code: '7' is 55 and '0' is 48. Printed with `%d`, c shows 55. Subtracting '0' gives 55 − 48 = 7, the digit's value. Output: 55 7.

7 7 treats '7' as the number 7; 7 0 also treats '0' as zero and so subtracts nothing; 55 55 forgets to subtract at all.

questions.q: `int a, b; a = (b = 4) + 2;` What are a and b afterwards?
questions.concept: Assignment yields the stored value
questions.why:
An assignment stores into its left operand and yields the value stored. `(b = 4)` stores 4 in b and has the value 4, so a = 4 + 2 = 6, and b stays 4.

a = 4, b = 4 ignores the + 2; a = 6, b = 6 gives b the outer result as well; a = 2, b = 4 treats the inner assignment as having no value.

questions.q: A sensor reading is either a whole-number count or a floating-point voltage, never both at once, and it needs no methods. Which construct fits?
questions.concept: Choosing between structure, union and class
questions.why:
A union's members all start at the same location, so it represents only one member at a time and wastes no space on the other. That is exactly a value that is one thing or the other, never both.

A struct gives both members their own storage and lets them hold values at once, which is more than is needed; a class adds methods, which the reading does not need; an array holds several items of the same type.

questions.q: Write a `struct Book` with members for a title (up to 40 characters), an author (up to 40 characters), the number of copies (a whole number) and the price (a decimal). Then define a variable `b` of that type and write two statements that set copies to 3 and price to 12.5 using the dot syntax.
questions.concept: Writing a structure and setting its members

questions.q: Write a class `Account` whose balance cannot be set directly from outside it: a private `balance`, a public `deposit(amount)` that adds to it, and a public `get_balance()` that returns it. Then say what happens to the line `a.balance = 1000;` written outside the class for an Account `a`.
questions.concept: Encapsulation with public and private

questions.q: A program must find the average of the first five multiples of 9. List the variables the problem needs, write a C definition for each (type then name, with its starting value where there is one), and write the one statement that computes the average so that the decimal part is not lost. State the value printed with `%.1f`.
questions.concept: Representing a problem as data
questions.why:
The problem needs the sum of the multiples (or the multiples themselves), how many there are, and the result:

```c
int sum = 9 + 18 + 27 + 36 + 45;   /* 135 */
int count = 5;
float average = (float) sum / count;
```

Printed with `%.1f` this gives 27.0. A correct answer defines an int sum (or five int multiples), an int count, a float or double average, and casts one operand to float before the division (`(float) sum / count`, `sum / (float) count` or `sum / 5.0` are all accepted). `float average = sum / count;` happens to give 27.0 here because 135 / 5 is exact, but it loses the decimal part in general and is marked wrong; `(float)(sum / count)` is also wrong.

questions.q: A `struct Dog` and a `union Dog` are both written with the same three members `char name[20]`, `char breed[20]` and `char colour[20]`. Explain, in terms of where the members sit in memory, why setting `breed` destroys `name` in one of them and not the other, and what it means that a union represents only one member at a time.
questions.concept: Structure versus union in memory
questions.why:
In the struct each member has its own location: name, breed and colour occupy three separate 20-byte blocks (60 bytes in all), so writing breed leaves name untouched and all three can hold values at once. In the union all members start at the same location: there is one 20-byte block and name, breed and colour are three names for it, so writing breed overwrites the bytes that held name.

'One member at a time' means the union's storage holds whichever member was written last; the others are not preserved, and the union does not record which member is current. A correct answer says the struct members have separate storage, the union members share one starting address, and that this is why the union's earlier member is lost. Saying the union stores all three but hides two of them is wrong.

checks.topic: Where Nigerian human rights sit in law, and the five common abuses with their figures and statute.

questions.q: Security services detain a journalist for reporting on political corruption, and the NBC is used to clamp down on radio and television stations. Which of the five common human rights abuses is this?
questions.concept: Identifying a human rights abuse from a scenario
questions.why: Detaining journalists for sensitive reporting and using regulatory oversight through the NBC to restrict broadcasters are the marks of the freedom of expression abuse, meaning the restriction of speech and press. Extra-judicial killing involves security forces using lethal or excessive force, as highlighted by #EndSARS. Domestic violence and child marriage are abuses within households and families, not against the press.

questions.q: A State fixes 18 as the minimum age of marriage for boys and 15 for girls, and enforces both ages strictly. Under international human rights law, this State is:
options: In violation, because the minimum age must be the same for boys and girls
Compliant, because a minimum age has been established and is enforced
Compliant, as long as no public official takes part in any child marriage
In violation only if it also fails to act with due diligence to prevent child marriage
questions.concept: Child marriage and the State's obligations
questions.why: A State violates international human rights law if it fails to establish a minimum age of marriage, enforce it, provide for and enforce the same minimum age for boys and girls, act with due diligence to prevent child marriage, or if it involves public officials in it. Setting different ages for boys and girls breaches the third condition on its own. Establishing and enforcing an age does not cure the inequality, keeping officials out of it addresses a separate condition, and the due diligence condition is an additional ground rather than a requirement for the violation.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs a human rights figure or statute with its correct detail?
options: 43% of girls in Nigeria are married before the age of 15
The Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act was signed into law in 2009
The National Human Rights Commission received 1,701,519 cases in 2021, up from 1,287,280 in 2020
About 367,000 complaints were received by the National Human Rights Commission in 2020
questions.concept: Figures and statute attached to the common abuses
questions.why: The NHRC received 1,701,519 cases of rights violations in 2021, higher than the 1,287,280 complaints of 2020, so the number rose. The 43% figure is girls married before their 18th birthday; 16% is the figure for before 15. The VAPP Act was signed into law in 2015; 2009 is the year of the Rules with shortcomings and inhibitions. The 367,000 figure is women and gender-related issues in 2021, not an NHRC complaint count.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the legal framework for human rights in Nigeria is correct?
options: The 1979 Constitution is where fundamental human rights are currently contained
The 2009 Rules are what make the rights enforceable in Nigerian courts
Article 1 of the UN Declaration of Human Rights forms part of Chapter IV of the Constitution
Human rights are contained in Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution, Sections 33 to 46
questions.concept: Where human rights sit in Nigerian law
questions.why: Human rights are contained in Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution, Sections 33 to 46. The 1979 Constitution introduced the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy and Fundamental Human Rights, but the rights now sit in the 1999 Constitution. It is the African Charter on Human and People's Rights that guarantees enforceability in Nigerian courts; the 2009 Rules are noted for their shortcomings. Article 1 of the UN Declaration supplies the definition of human rights, not a section of the Nigerian Constitution.

questions.q: What is a human rights abuse?
options: Anything that harms someone's human rights, including harm to people, communities and the environment
Any breach of an international treaty that a country has signed
An unlawful act committed only by the police or the military
A restriction on the media imposed by the National Broadcasting Commission
questions.concept: Definition of a human rights abuse
questions.why: A human rights abuse is anything that harms someone's human rights, and the harm can be to people, communities or the environment. It is not defined by treaties: human rights are not validated by the number of international treaties a country has signed. Security forces are implicated in extra-judicial killings but abuses can also come from non-state actors, and NBC restrictions are only one example of the freedom of expression abuse.
